https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/25/what.text: Hundreds of southern right whale calves have died in recent months in Argentine Patagonia, in an episode that has put scientists and authorities on alert. Initial investigations point to a bacterial infection as a possible cause of an exceptionally high mortality rate this season.Just this week, dozens of dead whale calves have appeared on beaches in the province of Chubut, in southern Argentina. Cases have been recorded since June, affecting one of this species' main breeding grounds in the South Atlantic."The mortality rate among calves is quite high, especially this season," explained Mariano Coscarella, a researcher at the Marine Mammals Laboratory of the National Scientific and Technical Research Council (Conicet), speaking to AFP.Bacteria among the main hypothesesVeterinarians are now investigating whether erysipelas, an infectious disease caused by bacteria that are often present on the skin of these mammals, could be behind the deaths.Authorities in Chubut have indicated that initial analyses point specifically to a common marine bacterium, although the investigation remains open to establish with certainty what is causing the fatalities.Coscarella believes that for the moment the evidence points to a natural cause, but warns that a possible influence of human activity still cannot be completely ruled out.The provincial government says it is working together with the scientific community to determine the origin of the episode.One of the southern right whale's main calving groundsPuerto Madryn and the nearby Valdés Peninsula form one of the major breeding refuges for the southern right whale. Every year, large numbers of whales arrive in these waters to mate and raise their young. These cetaceans can reach around 17 metres in length and weigh about 40 tonnes as adults.In 2025, a record 2,110 whales were counted in the area, around 800 of them juveniles. This year, the tally stands at 1,375 animals, including nearly 400 calves, according to data provided by Coscarella.Despite the high number of deaths recorded this season, the researcher notes that the episode does not, for now, pose a medium-term threat to the region's whale population.The species' longevity is one of the factors behind that assessment. Local authorities estimate that a southern right whale can live for around 60 years.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/15.text: Listen (2 mins) Save Share NATO jet shoots down suspected Russian drone over Lithuania on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google NATO has pledged more support for Ukraine as European leaders warn that Russia's war is expanding [File: AFP] By Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters Published On 15 Sep 2026 15 Sep 2026 An Italian fighter jet flying for NATO has brought down what officials said was a suspected Russian drone in Lithuanian airspace. According to Lithuania’s national crisis management centre, the drone entered the country’s airspace on Tuesday from Belarus and was shot down near the small settlement of Pratkunai in central Lithuania, just north of the country’s second-largest city, Kaunas. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Russia warns Denmark after near miss in Baltic Sea list 2 of 3 Ukraine drone strikes kill four as Russia attacks close to Poland border list 3 of 3 NATO pledges more Ukraine support after Russia strikes near Poland end of list Lithuania’s Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said on social media the drone was carrying an explosive. Debris from the device was being examined to determine if it was from Russia or another country. The intervention by the Italian fighter jet demonstrated “the value of the Atlantic alliance” and “what it means to be an ally”, Kaunas said after meeting crews who were at the scene. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the incident part of a pattern of “aggression and provocation” against Europe. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul laid the blame on Russia, saying that NATO members would not be intimidated. Russian officials did not immediately comment on the incident. Wider conflict The drone was intercepted over Lithuania after Russia fired flares at a Danish military helicopter monitoring a Russian warship in the Baltic Sea on Monday. In a post on X on Tuesday, Poland’s Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said, that “recent days show that Russia’s actions threaten the security of the entire Europe”. The escalations followed a series of Russian drone strikes on Sunday, prompting NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte to pledge more support for Ukraine. Russian drones hit a train close to the Polish border, minutes after a delegation of current and former officials from the United Kingdom, the United States and Europe passed through the station. Advertisement At a press conference, Kaunas warned that the Russia-Ukraine war has spread and that incidents would continue unless there was a negotiated settlement, but maintained that “Putin does not want” a peaceful settlement.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Australian Greens leader David Shoebridge said the party would only offer its support for the changes if the government excluded pensioners, prompting Mark Butler to say the new leadership had ‘spied a political opportunity’. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP View image in fullscreen Australian Greens leader David Shoebridge said the party would only offer its support for the changes if the government excluded pensioners, prompting Mark Butler to say the new leadership had ‘spied a political opportunity’. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP Australian politics Labor’s bill to cut private health insurance rebate blocked by Greens over pensioner carve-out Almost 80,000 older Australians expected to end private health cover by 2028-29 as a result of Albanese government’s proposal Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Tess Ikonomou Wed 14 Oct 2026 03.59 EDT Last modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 04.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Labor’s bid to cut the private health insurance rebate for over-65s has been blocked in parliament, with the Greens insisting they will withhold support unless pensioners receive a carve-out from the new rules. The proposed changes, which would take effect from April 2027, would save the federal budget $3bn. It marks another defeat for a key cost-saving measure after the government was forced to back down on its plan to cap allied health payments for veterans which would have saved $748m over three years. People who are 65 or over currently receive a larger rebate on their premium, with the rebate higher for those 70 and over. The Greens, Coalition and crossbench senators teamed up in the Senate on Wednesday to block Labor’s bill. In a rare move, the bill was discharged from the upper house, meaning it will need to be reintroduced if Labor tries to push ahead. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The health minister, Mark Butler, said the government planned to reintroduce the same bill to parliament on Thursday. “It is important that the parliament have a proper debate, that these really important questions for older Australians are not held hostage to political stunts, but instead that the elected members of the House of Representatives and elected senators take these issues seriously and debate them properly,” he said. Almost 80,000 older Australians are expected to ditch their private health cover by 2028-29 as a result of the Albanese government’s proposal, according to health department modelling released under freedom of information laws. The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, said the party would only offer its support for the changes if the government excluded pensioners. “We say to Labor, if you want to bring this bill back … [by] carving out 1.2 million pensioners from this attack … come and talk to us,” he said. “We will pass it in a heartbeat. But we will not be joining with Labor to punch down on pensioners in the middle of a cost of living crisis.” Butler said the new Greens leadership “spied a political opportunity” to team up with the Coalition. The chief executive of the Council on the Ageing Australia, Patricia Sparrow, rejected the planned savings being linked to aged care funding commitments. “Older Australians shouldn’t have to choose between protecting their health and paying for everyday essentials. Nor should they be asked to choose between affordable healthcare and a properly funded aged care system,” she said. The shadow health minister, Anne Ruston, said the policy would have affected up to 1.5 million pensioners. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “The idea that a government would have to cut the health system to need to pay for the aged care system … just reflects the fact of how much this government has lost control of their budget bottom line,” she said. Greens prepare for fight with Labor over social media algorithm reform, with ‘pervert glasses’ in its sights Read more The proposal has been criticised by the states and territories, which warn their health services will come under increasing pressure. The Victorian health minister, Ingrid Stitt, said she had raised concerns with Butler, vowing to oppose “any move that makes it harder for Victorians to get the care they need”. “Any commonwealth savings shouldn’t come at the expense of older Victorians or simply shift pressure on to our public hospitals,” she said. The New South Wales health minister, Ryan Park, said the state was already experiencing “significant pressure” on its public health system due to the commonwealth’s failure to provide sufficient aged care placements. “This is not good for [the aged] and they deserve better,” he said. The Queensland health minister, Tim Nicholls, said the “ additional pressure will come at the expense of the thousands of older Australians already stuck in hospitals right across the country”. The Tasmanian health minister, Bridget Archer, said the federal government was “already refusing to provide solutions to get aged care patients out of hospital and this dog of a policy will make things even worse”.
